# The brand new Onlook is here


### The updated open-source developer tool for designers has resurrected on GitHub


[Daniel Farrell](https://substack.com/@danielfarrell)


Nov 19, 2026


We just open-sourced the brand new version of Onlook. Before we get into what’s new, please go to the repository and support the project with a star ⭐


[Star Onlook on GitHub](https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook)


If you don’t know what GitHub stars are, they’re basically a “like” for a project. A lot of developers use them to decide whether something is worth a look, so every single one helps more than you’d think.


And if you have friends who are designers, or who’d be into this kind of thing, please send it their way and ask them to star it too.


We also just launched on Hacker News today. If you have a few minutes, find us on the launch page, give it a try, and drop a comment that contributes to the discussion (i.e. not a “Onlook is great!” but a “Why did you guys decide to do X instead of Y?” kind of comment).


Hacker News has been really good to us in the past (it’s a big part of how Onlook became the #1 trending repo on GitHub, twice), so please feel free to join in on the conversation (and grill us!).


## What’s new with Onlook


Onlook is the open-source developer tool for designers, and it’s been rebuilt entirely from the ground up, so if you tried an older version, this one is going to feel pretty different (in a good way, I hope).


[Download Onlook](https://www.onlook.com/)


The new version is a desktop app for Mac that puts a canvas on top of your real project. Not a mockup of it – your actual app, running locally with real data. You can import a repo from GitHub or open a local folder, and Onlook handles the setup for you.


From there, a few things I think you’ll like:


-


**Explore a ton of ideas at once** . Ask for every flow in your product, every state of a component, or ten versions of one screen, and they all show up side by side on the canvas. Each frame is a real browser running your app and you can jump to “Preview” mode to interact with it.


Explorations of a flipdot-display in the editor


-


**Design with your own intentionality.** Select an element, and ask the agent to “create a showcase of variations” of it, or “render 5 different styles as separate frames for how this could be implemented.” It’s almost like you’re creative-directing on top of code.


-


**Design the real product** . Your work happens on its own copy of the project, and every change is a normal pull request you can review, share with an engineer, or just throw away as an exploration.


-


**Create shareable Artifacts** . We introduced the ability to make quick HTML sketches that live outside your repo. You can “stamp” part of your interface into one, use it as a reference for another exploration, or send it to a coworker as an interactive export. I go back to mine all the time when I need ideas.


Showcasing Artifacts in the left panel that were created in Onlook


## Why we rebuilt it


The first version of Onlook was specifically built to run on React and Tailwind, and you could style things directly, but it…


1.


only worked on specific types of projects. And…


2.


was pretty slow to make edits on really big codebases. This was due to the mechanics of how we were able to locate specific elements.


Now that coding agents can read and edit basically any codebase, we rebuilt the whole thing around them, and gave designers the canvas to explore, arrange, and refine on top just like they’re used to.


We also tried a few things along the way that didn’t work (a web version of Onlook, and then another Storybook-native build after that). But the old desktop app kept getting hundreds of downloads a month without us promoting it at all, so we decided to go all in on a local-first app built for designing in code.


## Free and open source


The desktop app is free and the editor is open source. There’s no Onlook server between you and your code – it stays between you, your machine, and your agent. We’re Mac-only right now with Windows coming soon.


Eventually we’ll offer a paid cloud product for teams, but anything you can do on your own machine stays free.


A big part of why I’m excited to open-source this version is that designers can now really get their hands dirty with the code and make Onlook their own. and if you really want to get creative with it you can


[built it from source](https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook/) to customize it how you’d like.


Download the latest version of Onlook


[on our website here](https://www.onlook.com/install) :


[Download Onlook](https://www.onlook.com/install)


Designers have shifted the way they work into code, and we’re so excited to be sharing this editor with the community today. Code paired with AI is a new medium of creativity, and we think designers deserve a new tool that fits this reality of work.


Take the new editor for a spin, customize it, and push it to its limits – we can’t wait to see what you craft in Onlook!
